General Medication Instructions for Post-Surgical Patients

This document provides general guidance on taking medications prescribed after orthopedic surgery. Always follow your physician's or pharmacist's specific instructions, as they take precedence over this general guidance.

Taking Your Medications Safely:
Always take medications exactly as prescribed. Do not adjust doses or frequency without consulting your healthcare provider. Take oral medications with a full glass of water unless otherwise instructed. Some medications should be taken with food to reduce stomach upset — your prescription label or pharmacist will specify if this applies.

Pain Medications (Opioids):
Opioid pain relievers such as oxycodone or hydrocodone may be prescribed for moderate to severe post-surgical pain. These medications can cause drowsiness, constipation, and dizziness. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery while taking opioids. Avoid alcohol entirely when taking opioid medications, as the combination can be dangerous or fatal. These medications have a risk of dependence; use them only for as long as needed and taper under medical supervision.

Non-Opioid Pain Relievers (Acetaminophen):
Acetaminophen (e.g., Tylenol) may be prescribed or recommended for mild to moderate pain. Do not exceed 3,000 mg per day across all sources. Many combination medications contain acetaminophen — check all labels carefully to avoid unintentional overdose. Avoid alcohol when taking acetaminophen.

Anti-Inflammatory Medications (NSAIDs):
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen or naproxen may be recommended for pain and inflammation. These must be used with caution in post-surgical patients and should only be taken if specifically authorized by your surgeon. NSAIDs can increase bleeding risk and may interact with blood thinners such as warfarin. Always inform your provider of all medications you are taking before starting any NSAID.

Anticoagulants (Blood Thinners):
Blood thinners such as warfarin, rivaroxaban, or aspirin are commonly prescribed after joint replacement surgery to prevent blood clots. Take these medications at the same time each day. Do not miss doses. If you are on warfarin, you will need regular blood tests (INR monitoring) to ensure your dose is in the correct therapeutic range. Avoid foods high in vitamin K (such as leafy green vegetables) in large or variable quantities when on warfarin, as they can affect drug levels. Avoid all NSAIDs while on blood thinners unless explicitly approved by your doctor.

Antibiotics:
If you are prescribed antibiotics (e.g., cefazolin, amoxicillin), complete the full course even if you feel better. Do not share antibiotics with others. Be aware of potential side effects including upset stomach, diarrhea, and allergic reactions. Report any rash, hives, or difficulty breathing immediately.

Storage and Disposal:
Store all medications at room temperature unless otherwise specified, away from heat, moisture, and direct sunlight. Keep medications out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of unused or expired medications through an approved medication take-back program or as directed on the label.

Missed Doses:
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule. Never double up on doses. If you are unsure what to do, contact your pharmacy or healthcare provider.

Drug Interactions:
Many medications interact with each other. Inform your doctor and pharmacist of all prescription drugs, over-the-counter medications, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking. This is especially important for blood thinners, pain medications, and antibiotics, which have known interactions with many common substances.
